title: The poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3)
hook: blessed are the poor in spirit: the empty-handed have room for the kingdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus went up the mountain and sat down, an echo of Moses, and your line was sit down, listen.

Hashtag blessed. You've seen it under photos of a new car, a beach, a baby, a promotion. Blessed means things are going well. Back on that hillside, crowds have followed Jesus from all over, bringing their sick. He has just sat down. And the first words of the sermon are a list of people who are blessed. Only nobody on the list has a new car. It starts with the people who have nothing.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `THE FIRST WORDS OF THE SERMON.` → `IT STARTS WITH THE EMPTY-HANDED.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." This is the first of the Beatitudes. Matthew's Greek word for blessed is makarios: happy, fortunate, well off, the word Greeks used for the gods and the rich. Its Hebrew counterpart opens the book of Psalms: blessed is the man. So makarios is partly a congratulation. Lucky you. You're in a good place. Then look who he congratulates. The Greek word for poor here isn't a little short this month. It's the word for a beggar, someone with empty hands. Luke's version just says blessed be ye poor. Matthew adds in spirit, and Christians read that in more than one way. Some hear the humble: people who know they can't earn their way to God. Others hear the poor who have no pride left to hold on to. Some read both together. Either way, it's the opposite of self-sufficient. And the promise isn't someday. Theirs is the kingdom of heaven: present tense. Here's a picture that helps. You can't receive a gift with your hands full. Clutching your phone, your coffee and your bags, you have to put something down first. The poor in spirit already have their hands open. Maybe that's why this beatitude comes first. Everything else in the sermon is a gift, and empty hands can take it.
screen: `MAKARIOS: BLESSED, FORTUNATE.` · `POOR: A BEGGAR'S EMPTY HANDS.` · `IN SPIRIT: TWO READINGS.` · `THEIRS IS THE KINGDOM, NOW.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms open, facing up. Quietly name one thing you can't do on your own right now, help you need and haven't asked for, something you can't fix; no shame in it, your open hands already say I don't have everything. If you pray, you can bring that need to God with your hands open.
Blessed. Makarios in Greek: fortunate, well off, congratulations. And Jesus says it first to the poor in spirit.
Your line: empty hands can receive. The sermon starts with the empty-handed. Day two hundred thirty-three, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians know the Beatitudes by heart; Orthodox churches often sing them in the Divine Liturgy, and a number of churches read them on All Saints' Day.

notes: makarios used of the gods and the fortunate in classical Greek: standard lexicon claim; confirm phrasing 'the gods and the rich'.

Reviewer changed 'Hebrew cousin' to 'Hebrew counterpart': ashrei is not etymologically related to makarios, though the Septuagint renders ashrei with makarios. Also softened 'That's why this beatitude comes first' to 'Maybe', since the ordering rationale is interpretive.
ptochos (beggar, destitute) vs penes (working poor): standard distinction; confirm.
Readings of 'in spirit' are presented as held by different Christians without ranking.
Orthodox Divine Liturgy: the Beatitudes are sung as the third antiphon on many Sundays (typika); confirm phrasing 'most Sundays'.
